recipe.history:
Arugula — known as rucola in Italian, roquette in French, and rocket in British English — is a member of the Brassica family native to the Mediterranean basin and western Asia. Its use as a food plant dates to at least the first century CE in Rome, where it was prized both as a salad green and, curiously, as an aphrodisiac — it appears in love poetry and in agricultural texts alongside advice about which plants should be grown together in kitchen gardens. The distinctive peppery, slightly bitter bite of arugula comes from glucosinolates, the same family of compounds responsible for the pungency of mustard, radish, and horseradish. Wild arugula, a different species (Diplotaxis tenuifolia) from the cultivated varieties, is even more pungent and is still gathered from roadsides and hillsides throughout Italy, particularly in the south. In Italian cuisine, arugula is used both raw — tossed in salads with shaved Parmigiano and prosciutto, or scattered over pizza immediately after it comes from the oven — and very briefly wilted, where heat tames its bite and deepens its earthiness.

Arugula arrived on American plates via the Italian-American restaurant boom and the California cuisine revolution of the 1970s and 1980s. Chefs like Alice Waters at Chez Panisse championed arugula as a salad green with actual flavor, distinguishing it from the iceberg lettuce that had dominated American salads for decades. By the 1990s, the arugula-and-Parmesan combination had become a signature of American bistro cooking, and by the 2000s, a handful of arugula on a burger had become a signal of a restaurant's seriousness about its ingredients. The lemon dressing here — a simple emulsion of fresh lemon juice, good olive oil, and a touch of honey — keeps the arugula in conversation with itself, brightening its pepper notes and preventing the bitterness from reading as aggressive. Wild arugula, when available, intensifies everything.

Arugula is the green that convinced me greens on a burger were not affectation. I had always been skeptical — lettuce, I thought, added nothing but texture and water. Then someone put a dressed arugula salad on a burger at a restaurant, and the peppery, lemony tangle of leaves fundamentally changed how the burger tasted, cutting through the richness of the cheese and beef in a way I had never experienced with iceberg. I went home and immediately started putting arugula on every burger I made, experimenting with the dressing ratio and trying different cheeses to find the right partnership. Aged Pecorino Romano grated finely and tossed into the arugula with the lemon dressing became my standard — it melts slightly from the heat of the patty and adds a salty, sharp note that amplifies the arugula's own pungency.

Medium rare is the only rational choice for a burger topped with dressed arugula. The reasoning is about temperature and contrast: the cool, sharp, dressed greens need a warm, yielding counterpart beneath them to create the temperature and texture contrast that makes the combination interesting. A well-done patty at 160 degrees Fahrenheit would still be hot, but it would lack the yielding texture and rendered-fat richness that a medium-rare patty at 130 to 135 degrees provides. The lemon dressing acidulates slightly as it hits the warm meat, and the pepper of the arugula blooms in the steam rising from the pink interior. These are effects that can only happen when the patty is cooked correctly. Medium rare is not optional here — it is the mechanism by which the burger works.
ingredients: 1 small clove garlic, minced to paste
Fine sea salt and freshly cracked black pepper
Fine sea salt and white pepper
4 oz aged Pecorino Romano, shaved thin with a peeler
4 tbsp capers, drained and roughly chopped
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Bloom yeast in warm water with sugar for 5 minutes. Combine flour and salt in a stand mixer. Add yeast mixture, olive oil, and white wine vinegar; mix with dough hook on medium 8–10 minutes until smooth and slightly tacky. Cover; rise 1–1.5 hours until doubled.

2. Punch down, divide into 6 equal balls. Shape tightly; place on parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover; proof 45–60 minutes. Brush with water for a slightly crisp crust. Bake at 400°F for 16–18 minutes until golden and hollow-sounding. Cool on a rack.
3. Make the lemon aioli: Whisk egg yolks and Dijon. Stream in olive oil slowly, whisking constantly, until emulsified. Whisk in lemon juice and zest. Season with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate.
4. Make the lemon dressing: Whisk lemon juice, zest, honey, garlic paste, and Dijon together. Stream in olive oil whisking until emulsified. Season with salt and pepper.
5. Form the patties: Season ground chuck with salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Divide into 4 portions (8 oz each). Shape into 4.5-inch patties with a center dimple. Refrigerate 20 minutes.

6. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat with thin film of neutral oil. Cook patties undisturbed 3–4 minutes. Flip; top each with shaved Pecorino Romano slices. Cook 2–3 more minutes. Target 130–135°F for medium rare. Remove, tent with foil, rest 3 minutes.
7. Dress the arugula: Just before assembly, toss wild arugula with grated Pecorino Romano and enough lemon dressing to coat lightly. Season.
8. Toast bun halves cut-side down in butter or olive oil in a skillet until golden, about 90 seconds.

9. Assemble: Spread lemon aioli on both cut sides of the bun. Layer tomato slices on the bottom bun; season with flaky salt. Place the Pecorino-topped patty. Scatter capers and red onion slices. Mound the dressed arugula generously on top — it will tower; this is correct. Finish with a drizzle of leftover lemon dressing and more flaky sea salt. Crown with the top bun.
10. Serve immediately while arugula is freshly dressed.
